We are Mechatronics Engineering students passionate about space exploration, robotics, control systems, and embedded hardware. We offer solid skills in CAD, microcontroller programming, and rapid prototyping. We are looking for team members with experience in software/web development, satellite data analysis, or UI/UX and graphic design to build an impactful solution together!

Let's team up and build something amazing for this challenge!
summary:
Mexico Environmental Atlas is an interactive web platform that turns NASA satellite data into clear answers about how Mexico’s environment is changing. It maps four monthly variables across the whole country from 2004 to 2025: precipitation (GPM IMERG), tropospheric NO₂ (Aura OMI), evapotranspiration (MODIS MOD16) and land surface temperature (MODIS MOD11). All four are processed with each product’s quality filters and placed on a common 0.25° grid so they can be compared.

To be a true trend detective, the Atlas does more than show maps. For any location, state or municipality it calculates a robust trend (Theil–Sen slope with a Mann–Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation) and a 95% confidence interval. It then reports whether the change is a solid trend or could be explained by natural year-to-year variability.

It has two modes that share the same map: an Explorer mode for students and the public, with plain-language explanations and a glossary, and a Scientific mode with statistics, correlations, comparisons and data export.

Because the evidence is open, local and honest about uncertainty, citizens and decision-makers can act on real changes in water, air quality and heat. This supports the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals.
details:
Mexico Environmental Atlas is an interactive web platform that uses NASA satellite data to show how Mexico’s environment changed between 2004 and 2025. It maps four monthly variables across the whole country: precipitation from GPM IMERG, tropospheric NO₂ from Aura OMI, evapotranspiration from MODIS MOD16 and land surface temperature from MODIS MOD11. To make this possible, we process the data on Google Earth Engine and NASA Harmony and download only the area that covers Mexico. Each product goes through its official quality filters, missing values are never treated as zero, and all variables are placed on a common 0.25° grid so they can be compared fairly.

What makes the Atlas a true trend detective is that it goes beyond maps. For any point, state or municipality, it calculates a trend using a Mann–Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation, together with a 95% confidence interval. It then tells the user whether the change is a solid trend or something that could be explained by natural year-to-year variability. This turns complex satellite products into clear, local answers that are honest about their uncertainty. Anyone can explore maps, compare dates, study how two variables relate and download the results, with no technical background.

The project is also designed for very different audiences. Explorer mode uses plain language, guided questions and a glossary for students and the general public. Scientific mode adds statistics, metadata and data exports for researchers. Both share the same map, so switching between them keeps the selected place and date. Our goal is to help students, teachers, journalists and local governments see where rainfall, air quality, water use by vegetation and surface heat are truly changing. That evidence can guide decisions linked to the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, especially clean water, health, sustainable cities and climate action.

We built the platform with Python, using FastAPI, NumPy, xarray and rasterio for data processing and the API. The web interface was developed in TypeScript with React, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre and Plotly. All work was done in Visual Studio Code on standard laptops, with no special hardware. Throughout development, we respected the real availability of each dataset, flagged known issues such as the Terra satellite’s orbital drift, and never increased the resolution of any product. We also clearly separated demo data from real measurements, made the interface accessible and mobile-friendly, and kept credentials out of the code.
